chapter_theme: Songs at Kasi (காசி) on the Ganga: a sinner and gambler who never wore the holy ash asks to see the feet and gain jnana; a life traced from conception in the womb to the women who ruin it; and a body gone hollow like a wood-apple, with Murugan as the victor over the Jains.

651.reading: The poet confesses that he is a sinner on earth, a fool steeped in gambling, a thief of the mind's discipline, a vain man burning with desire who thought only of ways to keep spear-eyed women, a man of two deeds who never wore the true holy ash that the lovers of the full Sivajnana scriptures wear, and asks Murugan to smear it on him, let him see the red feet and grant the awakening of jnana. The praise names Vishnu who came when the crocodile seized the elephant, Siva who burned the three cities to ash, and Murugan who recited the Saiva scripture before the righteous, the jnana-speaking Kumara of the forest girl, at Kasi.
651.nuance: பூசு மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனைப் பூசி: the verb is repeated, 'me who did not smear it, smear', so the poet asks the god to put the ash on him himself. காரணக்குறியான நீதியரானவர்க்கு முன்னாகவே நெறி காவியச் சிவநூலை ஓதிய may refer to a particular telling of a Saiva text before an assembly; the allusion is not clear.

652.reading: The poet traces his making: the union of a man and a woman, the seed growing within by Brahma's will, the embryo taking shape like a grub, a ball, a palm fruit, a tender coconut and a pot by the way of deeds, ten months passing until it comes head down into the world, the parents calling it their child, the milk, the crawling and the toddling; then he asks whether he must perish through big-eyed women. The praise tells of Narasimha bursting from a pillar to tear Hiranya's body for the boy who said Hari was there, names Narayana of the conch and discus asleep on the serpent at Srirangam as uncle, and Parameswari at Siva's side as mother, at Kasi on the Ganga.
652.nuance: The growth of the embryo by stages of size (பந்து, பனைபழம், இளநீர், குடம்) and the tenth month head down (திங்கட் பதுசெல வேதலை கீழுற) is a formula the book repeats (see 520). The whole of the plea is the life story; the fault is named only in its last words, the women.

653.reading: A short song: the poet asks that, with his body become like a wood-apple eaten by an elephant and pervaded by infatuation, wearied daily like the boorish, he not be let to wither, but be given grace. The praise names Murugan the crest-jewel who won the debate when the Jain lords went to the stake, the hero on the peacock, son of Umapati of the dark throat, at Kasi by the Ganga.
653.nuance: வேழம் உண்ட விளாங்கனி: the proverbial wood-apple that the elephant leaves whole outside and empty within, an image of a body hollowed while it looks intact. அமணீசர்கள் கழுவேற வாதில் வென்ற is Sambandar's victory at Madurai, so Murugan is again identified with Sambandar (639, 641, 666).

links.note: Both trace the embryo growing through the sizes of a seed, palm fruit and coconut and slipping head down into the world, a formula the book repeats; 520 goes on to virtue forgotten and a stinking body, 652 to the women who ruin the grown child.
Both make the ten months in the womb the start of bondage: Tirumular's form grows mingled with maya, and 652's child, grown by the way of deeds, ends among women.

651 confesses he never wore the true holy ash (மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனை) and asks Murugan to smear it on him and let him see the red feet. Tirumular says those who wear the armour-ash gladly lose their deeds (தங்கா வினைகள்), reach the Siva state and join the beautiful feet (திருவடி சேர்வரே). The song's plea follows the Tirumanthiram's sequence exactly: ash, deeds ended, the feet.

Both use the wood-apple swallowed by the elephant, whole outside and empty within. In 653 it is the poet's body (வேழம் உண்ட விளாகனி அதுபோல மேனி) hollowed by delusion; in Tirumular Siva swallows soul, turiya and world like that fruit (கரியுண் விளவின் கனிபோல்). The same image is a ruin in the song and the Lord's taking-in in the Tirumanthiram.

source_issues: Song 653: one corrupt character in மயலு஡றி (line 338), probably மயலூறி.
